name: CO2 capture from coal power plant, offsite
notes:
Shell CANSOLV Post-Combustion CO2 Capture System (95% CO2 Capture)

Reference: DOE/NETL-DOE/NETL-2023/4320
Schmitt, Tommy, Leptinsky, Sarah, Turner, Marc, Zoelle, Alexander, White, Charles W., Hughes, Sydney, Homsy, Sally, Woods, Mark, Hoffman, Hannah, Shultz, Travis, and James III, Robert E.. Cost and Performance Baseline for Fossil Energy Plants Volume 1: Bituminous Coal and Natural Gas to Electricity. United States: N. p., 2022. <https://doi.org/10.2172/1893822>.


1. Purpose of Each Energy Input (from top to bottom)
    a) Electricity - CO2 capture system
    b) Natural Gas - Steam generation for CO2 capture system
    c) Electricity - CO2 compression after capture
    d) Electricity - CO2 pipeline transportation electricity for booster pump(s)

2. Zero natural gas input for power plant CO2 sources:
    The use of natural gas is to produce steam for the CO2 capture system. Because power plants are already producing steam for electricity generation, there is no extra natural gas input for steam production.  
    Instead, the loss of the steam for CO2 capture is accounted for by additional electricity demand for CO2 capture, which is the reduction of the total growth generation of power plants. 
    This results in the higher electricity demand for CO2 capture compared to the industrial CO2 sources like Hydrogen, Cement, and Iron & Steel.

3. Electricity for CO2 pipeline transportation
    a) This is to deliver CO2 by a 200-miles pipeline with one booster pump.
    b) The electricity demand for one booster pump is 7.653541 MJ/metric ton of CO2 with the following conditions: 
        - Pressures fixed: 2200 psia and 1500 psia 
        - Transportation temperature = 25 degC
        - Booster pump efficiency = 70%
        - # of booster: at every 100 miles
